Hypertrophic Scar vs Keloid

Overview

Both of these scars form due to excess collagen deposition during wound healing

Hypertrophic scar

Raised scar that don’t grow beyond the boundaries of the original wound

Maybe associated with itchiness and pain

Develops due to trauma, wounds …

Hypertrophic scar ranges in color from red to brown

Develop 4 weeks after injury and continues to thicken for up to six months

Often regresses in one or two years

Tension and flexor areas and restrict movement if they are located near a joint

Treatment using cryosurgery and silicon sheeting maybe helpful

Keloid scar

Firm, rubbery lesions or shiny, fibrous nodules that can be sometimes itchy and painful

Form because of injury or a wound and usually after 3 months to years of the initial insult, but sometimes arise spontaneously

Autosomal dominant predisposition

They Extend beyond original wound

Color vary from pink to dark brown

Rarely regress spontaneously

Keloid scar is benign

Need multimodal approach for treatment

Surgical excision

Steroids

Silicone sheets

Cryosurgery

Table from slide 9
Hypertrophic scar Keloid
Size Stay within the initial wound Grow beyond the initial wound
Onset Develop 4 weeks after injury and continues to thicken for up to six months Forms after 3 months to years of the initial insult and grow over time
Offset Shrink after a year Don’t shrink at all
Effect on joint movmenet Can restrict joint movement Don’t restrict joint movement at all
Incidence More common Less common
Location Grow anywhere in the body where the wound is Commonly develop on the upper torso, earlobes and cheeks
